items.title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
items.summary_1line: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Pr...
items.editor_note: Opens the voice angle: can the agent tell the active user from TV audio or colleagues in under a second.

items.title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
items.summary_1line: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be...
items.editor_note: Adds the security angle: malicious instructions from one session persisting through agent memory into later ones.

items.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
items.summary_1line: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks...
items.editor_note: Moves the real-world framing to infrastructure: long-horizon optimization tasks for agents.

items.editor_note: Extends voice evaluation to full-duplex work, where users redirect the agent mid-task.

items.editor_note: Replication study: agents sharing memory coordinate without being told to, a safety and engineering concern.

items.title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
items.summary_1line: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone task...
items.editor_note: Applies the framing to research agents, scoring delivery inside real researcher sessions.

items.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
items.summary_1line: Coding agents increasingly review code, yet whether they catch the privacy defects that laws such as the GDPR require software to avoid remains largely untested, partly because few datasets connect real privacy defect...

items.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
items.summary_1line: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate oppo...
items.editor_note: Adds video: agents must act on high-frame-rate footage to gather evidence.

items.title: $μ$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents
items.summary_1line: μ-Bench is a benchmark of 800 simulated multi-user voice-agent cases across 20 domains, testing joint task completion; across 13 agents, proprietary systems reach about 62–65% success while open-weight models stay below 20%.
items.editor_note: Quantifies a model gap: proprietary voice agents near 62–65%, open-weight below 20% on multi-user tasks.

editorial.tldr: This is a research trend, not one event: unrelated arXiv papers since Nov 6 each test agents on real sessions, real tools or real fixes instead of standalone tasks. It began with memory poisoning and voice-agent speaker separation, then moved to long-horizon infra work, researcher workspaces, privacy-aware code review (Nov 13) and agentic video (Nov 18).
editorial.whats_new: μ-Bench (Nov 25) tests voice agents serving several users at once across 800 simulated cases in 20 domains; proprietary agents reach about 62–65% success while open-weight models stay below 20%.
editorial.why_it_matters: Each paper argues that standalone task scores overstate how agents behave on stateful, multi-party, long-horizon or compliance-sensitive work, and μ-Bench puts a 40-point gap between proprietary and open-weight voice agents on exactly that kind of work.
editorial.take_for_builders: If you ship a voice agent on an open-weight model, test it on multi-speaker sessions before rollout; if your agents persist memory, add an eval that replays a poisoned instruction across sessions.

beats.headline: MemoryDojo shows agent memory is an attack surface
beats.summary: Malicious instructions can persist across sessions through memory; companion papers study coordination through shared memory and evolve memory designs as programs.

beats.headline: Voice-agent benchmarks move past single-turn speech
beats.summary: One measures whether speaker embedders isolate the active user from background speech in under a second; Joi-Bench-Task tests task coordination while the user interrupts or redirects.

beats.headline: Infrathon and ARE-bench test agents on sustained real work
beats.summary: Agents optimize real AI infrastructure and deliver inside real researcher workspaces; a systems paper cuts batch makespan for running these agent workloads.

beats.headline: PrivacyPR targets privacy defects in agent code review
beats.summary: A dataset linking real privacy fixes to the defects they repaired, aimed at coding agents that review pull requests.

beats.headline: VideoACE asks agents to act on high-frame-rate video
beats.summary: Scores whether agents interact with a video environment to gather evidence, not just answer questions about clips.

beats.headline: μ-Bench: multi-user voice agents, with a wide open-weight gap
beats.summary: 800 simulated shared-interaction cases across 20 domains and 13 agents; proprietary systems reach about 62–65% success, open-weight models stay below 20%.

open_questions: Will any of these benchmarks publish a public leaderboard with frontier-model scores?
Does MemoryDojo show poisoned memory surviving into later sessions for the memory systems teams actually ship?
Do agents that score well on standalone suites rank lower on Infrathon or ARE-bench, as the authors suggest?
What share of PrivacyPR's real privacy defects do current coding-agent reviewers catch?
Does μ-Bench's open-weight gap come from the base model or from the voice-agent scaffolding around it?
Will the datasets and harnesses be released openly enough to rerun as internal evals?
